prompt_free_text:
This paper tackles an important and practically relevant problem: extracting product attributes in an open-world setting with only light supervision. The proposed setting goes beyond closed-world tagging and even beyond zero-shot extraction with predefined target types, by asking the system to both expand known attribute types and discover previously unseen ones automatically. This is a meaningful formulation for e-commerce, where attribute vocabularies evolve quickly and exhaustive annotation is expensive. The paper also contributes a new dataset, WoaM, and a method, Amacer, that combines seed-supervised contrastive learning, syntax-based candidate generation, adaptive expansion for known attributes, and two forms of weak regularization for unseen attribute discovery. Overall, I found the problem well motivated, the empirical gains substantial, and the paper potentially impactful. At the same time, there are several methodological and evaluation issues that should be clarified or strengthened before I would consider the work fully convincing at a top-tier venue.

The strongest aspect of the paper is the task formulation itself. The distinction between expanding existing seed attributes and discovering entirely new attribute types is sensible and closer to real deployment than standard closed-world extraction. The paper also correctly identifies that requiring explicit descriptions of unseen types, as in zero-shot settings, is still restrictive. Framing the output as clusters rather than named labels is a reasonable choice for evaluation under this open-world assumption. This is a genuine conceptual contribution, and the dataset appears designed to reflect it, especially by including both titles and bullet points and by emphasizing the much higher novelty and lower density in bullet points.

The dataset contribution is promising, but it also raises several concerns. On the positive side, the authors attempt to strike a balance between scalability and quality by constructing a curated seed set from retailer profiles and separately annotating a test set for open-world evaluation. The inclusion of four categories and the explicit reporting of unseen type/value ratios are useful. However, the scale and diversity are still somewhat limited for a paper making broad claims about open-world product attribute mining. Four categories from a single marketplace and a single language may not be enough to establish generality. More importantly, the paper does not provide enough detail on annotation quality for the test set. It mentions two in-house annotators, but I did not see inter-annotator agreement, adjudication procedures, annotation guidelines, or examples of difficult boundary/type decisions beyond a few qualitative cases. Since the evaluation depends heavily on subjective judgments about what counts as a “reasonable attribute value” and how new types are defined, stronger evidence of annotation reliability is necessary.

The proposed method is intuitive and modular. The syntax-based candidate generation is simple but well motivated, especially given the limitations of segmentation-based methods on bullet points. The use of POS patterns mined from product profiles is a clever way to inject weak structural bias without requiring extensive manual engineering. The supervised contrastive objective over seed values is also a natural fit for the seed expansion subproblem, and the adaptive expansion stage is a reasonable mechanism for assigning candidates to known seed types before clustering the remainder. The two regularization components for unseen attributes are the most novel part: a self-supervised bullet-point co-occurrence heuristic and a latent-attribute topic-model-inspired objective over candidate spans. These ideas are plausible and align with the goal of extracting implicit semantic structure from product context.

That said, the novelty of the modeling contribution is somewhat incremental at the component level. Most pieces are adaptations of existing ideas: supervised contrastive learning, DBSCAN, support-set thresholding, skip-gram-like co-occurrence heuristics, and neural topic modeling. The contribution lies more in the combination and task-specific formulation than in a fundamentally new algorithmic idea. That is acceptable if the empirical validation is strong, but then the paper needs especially careful ablations and analysis to isolate what truly matters. The current experiments go part of the way, but not far enough.

The empirical results are encouraging. Amacer improves substantially over OA-Mine and tagging baselines, especially on the proposed open-world setting. The gains in the main pseudo-F1 metric are large, and the decomposition by seed versus new types suggests that the regularization is particularly helpful for unseen attributes, which supports the paper’s central claim. The comparison between segmentation-based and syntax-based candidate generation is also useful and practically relevant. I also appreciated the additional span-only evaluation in Table 5 and the “gold candidates” analysis in Table 4, which help disentangle candidate generation from clustering quality.

However, the evaluation methodology is also the paper’s biggest weakness. The main metric is a “pseudo-F1” constructed by averaging Jaccard, ARI, and NMI as a proxy for precision and combining that with recall. This is unconventional and difficult to interpret. Jaccard, ARI, and NMI are clustering similarity measures with different statistical properties; averaging them and treating the result as precision is not theoretically justified. Because the paper’s headline improvements are reported in this pseudo-F1, the conclusions depend on a metric that may not correspond to any standard notion of extraction quality. The authors do report the underlying clustering metrics and recall separately, which helps, but the paper should either justify this aggregate much more carefully or avoid centering the evaluation around it. At minimum, the paper should report standard extraction metrics more prominently, perhaps separating span detection, assignment to known types, and discovery of novel clusters. For open-world clustering, metrics such as B-cubed precision/recall/F1, pairwise F1, or cluster-level purity/coverage might be more interpretable.

Relatedly, the evaluation of “new attribute discovery” remains somewhat indirect. The paper claims discovery of values from 39% of unseen attribute types, but this is not the same as correctly inducing coherent new clusters corresponding to meaningful new types. The qualitative example in Table 6 actually shows a common failure mode: unseen location-related attributes are extracted but absorbed into existing seed types. This suggests that the system may be better at broad attribute-like span extraction than at true novel type induction. I would have liked a more explicit evaluation of novel cluster quality: for example, how many induced non-seed clusters align predominantly with a single gold unseen type, how many unseen gold types are split across many clusters, and how often unseen values are incorrectly attached to seed clusters. Without such analysis, the claim of “new attribute discovery” feels somewhat stronger than what is fully demonstrated.

There are also some fairness questions in the baseline comparisons. The paper compares against OA-Mine in both its original segmentation setting and a modified OA-Mine* using the authors’ syntax-based candidates. This is useful, but it also highlights that candidate generation is a major source of gains. Since Amacer’s pipeline differs from OA-Mine in multiple places at once, it is hard to know how much of the improvement comes from better candidates, better contrastive learning, adaptive expansion, or the new regularizers. The paper does include Amacer-R and OA-Mine*, which partially addresses this, but I still think the ablation should be more systematic. For example, what happens with Amacer using only supervised contrastive learning plus DBSCAN, without adaptive expansion? What is the effect of self-supervised regularization alone versus latent attributes alone on both seed and new types? The paper states that latent attributes contribute around 70% of the improvement, but the exact supporting numbers are not shown in the main text. A clearer additive ablation table would strengthen the claims considerably.

Another concern is the dependence on candidate generation quality and external POS tagging. The paper acknowledges this limitation, and Table 5 indeed shows low span extraction precision and exact-match F1 across methods. This suggests that the overall system is bottlenecked by candidate quality. While the syntax-based approach is efficient and apparently better than segmentation, it may also encode a strong bias toward noun/adjective phrase-like attributes and miss attributes expressed in more varied syntactic forms. Since the task is open-world, recall over structurally unusual attributes matters. It would be helpful to know candidate-generation recall against gold spans, broken down by attribute type and by title versus bullet points. The “gold candidates” experiment hints at the upper bound, but a direct candidate-stage evaluation would make the pipeline limitations much clearer.

The latent attribute module is interesting, but currently under-validated. The paper motivates it as topic modeling over candidate spans and shows a few qualitative latent attributes, some of which are coherent. But there are several unanswered questions. How sensitive is performance to the number of latent attributes K? How severe is topic collapse in practice, and does it reduce downstream gains? Are the learned latent attributes category-specific or shared across categories? Is the module trained jointly with BERT end-to-end, and if so, how stable is optimization? Since this component is one of the paper’s main novelties, more analysis would be valuable. In particular, I would like to see whether the latent attributes improve representation geometry in a measurable way, for example via nearest-neighbor purity on unseen types or cluster separability diagnostics.

The paper is generally understandable, but the presentation could be improved. There are many grammatical errors and typos throughout, some of which make technical details harder to parse. Examples include repeated subject-verb agreement issues, inconsistent terminology, and awkward phrasing in the method and dataset sections. The equations are mostly clear, though the supervised contrastive loss notation appears slightly nonstandard and should be checked carefully; in particular, the denominator definition and whether positives are excluded/included should be made explicit. The adaptive thresholding equations also deserve more intuition: why should average intra-seed cosine distance define the acceptance threshold, and how robust is this when seed sets are small or heterogeneous? More discussion of computational cost would also help, especially since the method includes BERT encoding, contrastive learning, and a latent-variable objective over products and spans.

I also think the paper should discuss more explicitly what “attribute type” means operationally in annotation and evaluation. In e-commerce, the boundary between attributes, entities, and free-form descriptive phrases can be fuzzy. For example, “living room,” “vegetarian,” “virtually invisible,” and “moto g pure” appear among latent attributes or candidate spans, but whether these correspond to canonical product attributes may depend on schema design. Since the task is framed as open-world discovery of “reasonable attributes,” the paper needs a stronger ontology or at least clearer annotation principles to avoid the impression that the task is partly subjective clustering of salient phrases.

Despite these concerns, I think the paper has real merit. The problem is important, the dataset could be useful to the community, and the method appears practically effective. The strongest evidence in favor of acceptance is that the paper moves beyond standard closed-world extraction in a realistic direction and demonstrates nontrivial gains under limited supervision. The main reasons for hesitation are the unconventional evaluation metric, limited annotation-quality reporting, and insufficiently disentangled ablations for the proposed components.

My recommendation is borderline positive if the venue values practical task formulation and dataset contribution, but with clear reservations. To strengthen the paper, I would strongly encourage the authors to revise the evaluation around more standard and interpretable metrics, provide annotation agreement and guidelines, add a fuller ablation isolating candidate generation, adaptive expansion, self-supervised regularization, and latent attributes, and include more direct analysis of true unseen-type induction rather than aggregate clustering quality alone. If these issues are addressed, the work could become a solid contribution.

Some concrete questions for the authors that should be answered in a rebuttal or revision are as follows. First, can you provide inter-annotator agreement and more detail on adjudication for the test set, especially for unseen types? Second, can you justify the pseudo-F1 metric more rigorously, or alternatively report a standard clustering/extraction F1 as the primary metric? Third, what is candidate-generation recall and precision before clustering, and how much does it vary across categories and unseen types? Fourth, can you provide a clean ablation table with separate effects of syntax candidates, supervised contrastive learning, adaptive expansion, self-supervised regularization, and latent attributes? Fifth, how sensitive is the latent attribute module to K and to random initialization, and how often do you observe topic collapse? Sixth, can you quantify novel type induction more directly, for example by measuring purity/coverage of induced non-seed clusters against gold unseen types?

In summary, this is a thoughtful and practically motivated paper with a useful new setting and promising empirical results. Its main weaknesses are not in motivation but in validation and evaluation design. I appreciate the ambition and believe the work is close to being compelling, but it needs stronger methodological rigor around how success in open-world attribute discovery is measured and attributed.

prompt_structured_json.summary: The paper introduces a new lightly supervised open-world product attribute mining setting, where the goal is both to expand values for known seed attribute types and to discover entirely new attribute types without explicit type descriptions. To support this setting, the authors construct the WoaM dataset over four Amazon product categories with a curated seed set and human-annotated test set. They propose Amacer, a pipeline consisting of syntax-based candidate span generation using POS patterns, supervised contrastive representation learning from seed attributes, adaptive expansion for assigning candidates to seed types, DBSCAN for discovering additional clusters, and two auxiliary regularizers for unseen attributes: a self-supervised bullet-point co-occurrence contrastive loss and a neural latent-attribute reconstruction objective. Experiments show improvements over OA-Mine and tagging baselines on their proposed evaluation, with especially notable gains in recall and new-attribute discovery.
strengths: Addresses an important and practically relevant problem setting beyond closed-world and zero-shot extraction: discovering new attribute types under limited supervision.
Introduces a new dataset tailored to the proposed setting, including titles and bullet points, which is more realistic than title-only setups.
The overall system design is intuitive and modular: candidate generation, representation learning, seed expansion, and residual clustering are clearly separated.
The use of syntax-based candidate generation is simple, efficient, and empirically stronger than segmentation-based candidates in this benchmark.
The paper includes useful ablations comparing segmentation vs syntax candidates, with and without regularization, and decomposition by seed/new types and title/bullet-point subsets.
The latent-attribute regularization is a reasonable attempt to inject unsupervised semantic structure for unseen attributes, and qualitative examples suggest it learns meaningful concepts.
Code and data availability improve reproducibility.
weaknesses: The evaluation protocol is unconventional and somewhat weakly justified: the main metric is a pseudo-F1 built from averaging Jaccard, ARI, and NMI as a proxy for precision, which lacks a clear theoretical grounding.

The proposed supervised contrastive loss appears to be incorrectly formulated, with the denominator excluding positives and possibly the anchor itself, deviating from standard supervised contrastive learning; this raises concerns about implementation correctness or notation accuracy.

The paper conflates several sources of improvement—candidate generation quality, representation learning, adaptive expansion, and regularization—making it difficult to isolate the true contribution of the novel latent/self-supervised objectives.
The empirical scope is limited to only four product categories from Amazon, so claims about open-world generality and scalability are only partially supported.

Candidate generation relies heavily on POS tagging and patterns extracted from product profiles, which may encode domain-specific biases and may not transfer well to noisier domains or other languages.
The method still struggles substantially on exact span extraction and new-type discovery, with relatively low span precision and only partial coverage of unseen types.

Several methodological details are underspecified, including clustering hyperparameter sensitivity, batch construction for contrastive losses, and how duplicate spans across contexts are handled in training and clustering.
Writing quality is uneven, with many grammatical issues and some notation inconsistencies that make technical verification harder.
methodological_flaws: The supervised contrastive objective in Section 4 is mathematically suspicious. Standard supervised contrastive learning uses a denominator over all non-anchor examples, including positives; here the denominator is defined only over negatives. This changes the optimization substantially and may make the cited connection to Khosla et al. inaccurate. If this is only a notation error, the paper should clarify; if implemented as written, the method is not the claimed objective.

The same issue appears in the self-supervised contrastive loss in Section 6.1, again using only negatives in the denominator. This weakens confidence in the mathematical correctness of the training objective.

The adaptive expansion threshold uses the average pairwise cosine distance among seed values, scaled by delta, as an acceptance threshold. This heuristic is not theoretically justified and may behave counterintuitively when seed sets are heterogeneous or small; no sensitivity or failure analysis is provided.

The main evaluation metric ('pseudo precision' from averaged Jaccard/ARI/NMI combined with recall into pseudo-F1) is not a standard or validated measure of extraction-plus-clustering quality. Because clustering metrics and recall capture different phenomena and are not calibrated as precision/recall analogues, the resulting F1 may be misleading.

The comparison to closed-world tagging baselines is not entirely fair for the claimed task, since those models are structurally incapable of discovering new types; their inclusion is informative but should not be overinterpreted as evidence of superiority on the full problem.

The seed set and POS patterns are both derived from product profiles originating from the same ecosystem as the corpus, which may leak substantial domain structure into the lightly supervised setup. This does not invalidate the task, but it weakens claims of minimal supervision and open-world discovery.

Statistical significance claims are only briefly mentioned ('t-test >95% confidence') without specifying the unit of analysis, number of runs, variance across seeds, or whether assumptions of the test are satisfied. Given only four categories, significance evidence is weak.

The latent-attribute model is acknowledged to suffer from topic collapse, but the paper does not quantify its severity or analyze whether gains come from meaningful latent structure versus generic regularization effects.
